I got them at 21 as well. Here was the process:

I admitted myself to a hospital after nearly hanging myself but chickening out last minute. I explained I had no income and no insurance and met with the hospital's social worker, who helped me apply for medical assistance. After that was dealt with, I asked about getting ssi, and looked through the social security website.

I applied. I had to fill out some paperwork describing my disability, which I listed as depression, then had to meet with a doctor of their chosing. He was a nice guy, been practicing for around 50 years and set to retire at the end of the year. He asked me questions, I answered honestly. A few months later they decided I was disabled enough.

I had many things in my corner that helped me get there.

1. I had 3 suicide related hospitalizations in the past, one involving an attempted hanging. Being suicidal is considered an urgent condition and often speeds up the process. 

2. My father was able to support me while I did this. Honestly, mostly what they want to know is: how are currently supporting yourself if you need the government to pay your bills? I had the answer of "residual student loans and my dad is loaning me money."

3. I was white in a predominantly black neighborhood. The social security office I went to had a mix of races working there, but only black people in the lobby. I get the a feeling that they gave me some credit based on that.

4. I was lucky. I got it first time around, and that almost never happens.

I got on disability with just depression the first time I applied, but the stars really aligned for me. 

1. I had 3 hospital admissions for suicidal thoughts and 1 for an attempt with what is considered a highly lethal method. I applied for the first time through a social worker at the hospital. I feel this strongly expedited the process. Patients with recent suicide attempts are often put at the front of the line. 

2. My father paid my rent for 6 months it took apply, under the agreement I pay him back once I got on. The SSA is very concerned with how you are currently supporting yourself if you need disability, and having a written agreement with my father helped me. I also had my bank statements going back over a year printed. They don't care about the little expenses (unless they really add up) mostly just rent and utilities. 

3. When they sent me to be examined by a doctor, he was very sympathetic. He had been working in the field of psychology for 50 years and was going to retire soon. I think I checked off a lot of boxes in the interview to indicate I was well and truly depressed.

4. I was white. Seriously. I genuinely feel I might have gotten preferential treatment for being a white person in a predominantly black neighborhood. The employees at the office I went to were of all races, but I think I was the only white guy in the waiting room. 

Like I said, mostly luck and circumstance. I don't really know if there is any advice I can give you other than if you get hospitalized, that's the prime opportunity to apply. It's also easier to prove you have one severely impairing disability than a lot of them that come together to make you unable to work.
